The local estimate and Zen are not using the same tier cutoff, and Zen’s cutoff is not the one in the docs.

Go’s published Luna/Grok table is ≤272K / >272K:

https://opencode.ai/docs/go/#usage-limits

Zen still flips on a hardcoded 200 000 of `input + cacheRead + cacheWrite5m + cacheWrite1h`:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/console/app/src/routes/zen/util/handler.ts#L1035-L1039

On GPT-5.6 Luna the Usage History “Input” column is that same sum (`usage-section.tsx`), and `inputTokens` and `cacheWrite5mTokens` differ by 3 on almost every row — they are the same uncached tokens counted twice. So the 200k trip is really ~100k of actual prompt plus a write duplicate.

A 302-request Luna burst on 2026-08-18 classified cleanly: every request with that sum ≤193k billed at the low tier, every request ≥202k billed at the high tier. 94 requests sat in 200–272k and paid the high rate. Versus the documented 272k rule that is **+$2.53** on one afternoon.

That is the same class of “UI used the cheap tier, invoice used the expensive one” as the $3.37 vs $3.71 in this report. The one-line fix is to stop using `200_000` and read `cost.tiers[0].tier.size` (272 000 for Luna / Grok / the GPT-5.6 family), and to decide the tier on `input + cacheRead` — not on input+read+write.

The TUI is not “about half by rounding.” It is subtracting Luna’s cache-write tokens from a total that never contained them as extra, and the web is not doing that subtraction.

Your own capture is enough:

```
OpenAI Luna
  inputTokens:              82,307
    noCacheTokens:               3
    cacheReadTokens:        79,354
    cacheWriteTokens:        2,950

  3 + 79,354 + 2,950 = 82,307
```

So `inputTokens` is already the whole prompt: fresh + read + write. It is not exclusive of the write.

TUI then shows:

```
Total input:    85,257     = 82,307 + 2,950   (write added again)
Input:           2,953     = 82,307 − 79,354  (write still inside)
Cached write:    2,950
```

`getUsage` then does the Anthropic split:

```
fresh = inputTokens − cacheRead − cacheWrite
      = 82,307 − 79,354 − 2,950
      = 3
```

Those 2,950 write tokens were already inside `82,307`. Subtracting them again leaves 3 tokens at the input rate instead of 2,953. Anthropic looks right because its `inputTokens` *is* exclusive of cache, so the same minus does not eat a second copy.

The web path does not subtract the write. Zen only removes the cache read:

```
input billed = prompt_tokens − cached_tokens   → 82,307 − 79,354 = 2,953
```

plus 2,950 at the write rate. Same tokens, two bills on the web, one bill (write only) on the TUI.

On this request that is 2,950 tokens at Luna’s input price that the TUI never charges:

```
low tier   2,950 × $0.20 / 1M = $0.0006
high tier  2,950 × $0.40 / 1M = $0.0012
```

One row is small. A long session is thousands of those writes, which is the “TUI looks like half the web” screenshot.

This is not an OpenAI bug. `3 + 79,354 + 2,950 = 82,307` is internally consistent. The bug is applying the exclusive split (`input − read − write`) to a provider whose `inputTokens` is already inclusive. Handle it on the OpenAI / Luna mapper: if `noCache + read + write == inputTokens`, take `noCache` as fresh and do not subtract write a second time.

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/ai/src/protocols/openai-chat.ts#L582-L589

$3 of Grok against a 100% rolling bar is the Usage column, not a broken $12 cap.

https://opencode.ai/docs/go/#usage-limits

Grok 4.5’s **Usage** value is $15, so the shared windows are consumed at 4×:

```
$3 × (60 / 15) = $12
$12 / $12 rolling = 100%
```

That is the same identity as $3.65 of DeepSeek V4 Pro → 24% monthly (#43149) and $7.52 of qwen3.8-max → 100% weekly (#41146). The bars do not read Usage History dollars. They read `visible cost × (60 / model Usage)`.

Worked arithmetic for a full set of three bars is on #41391. This report is the clean Grok instance of it.

The 1-hit-in-8 table is the gateway reshuffling the upstream, not a 5-minute TTL and not the custom-provider assembler.

A session is only pinned when the model catalog sets `stickyProvider`. Otherwise the tracker returns immediately:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/console/app/src/routes/zen/util/stickyProviderTracker.ts#L4-L10

Selection then hashes the last four characters of the session id over the *current* provider pool (TPM / TPS / budget filters change that length live):

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/console/app/src/routes/zen/util/handler.ts#L643-L653

That is why a stable `ses_*`, a byte-identical system prompt, and `setCacheKey: true` still miss. The miss is decided after the client. OpenCode CLI and openclaw both hit it because they share the Go/Zen endpoint.

#35402 already showed the same hop on GLM-5.2 with byte-identical requests (usage JSON shape flipping between two upstreams). This report is that mechanism on the custom-provider path, with a cost table: one $0.046 hit vs seven ~$0.24 misses.

`setCacheKey` / `promptCacheKey` cannot fix it — Go’s oa-compat path does not pin on that field. `stickyProvider: "prefer"` on `glm-5.2` does. Compare `provider` on the one cheap row vs the seven expensive ones; if they differ, that is the whole ticket.

The 1.18.15 `serialize()` flatten made the payload denser with `[Assistant tool call]` lines. The reason a reasoning model then emits 40–60 tokens of thinking and `stop` is that compaction still goes out with **no system prompt**.

`PROMPT_COMPACTION` is registered on a hidden agent and never sent. The only assignment is here; there is no other reference in the tree:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/core/src/plugin/agent.ts#L143-L147

The request itself is one user message, `tools: []`, no `system`, no `generation.maxTokens`:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/core/src/session/compaction.ts#L274-L281

`title.ts` resolves its hidden agent and ships `PROMPT_TITLE` (which says “Never use tools”). Compaction does not. A Kimi reasoning model handed a wall of tool traces, with tools silently gone and nothing saying so, continues the trace instead of summarizing it. `finish: stop` + 0 text parts is that outcome. The empty summary then replaces history.

Same failure on DeepSeek is #42363 / #42371. The docs already claim “tools disabled and at most 4096 output tokens”; only the `tools: []` half exists. Passing `agent.info.system` (and `generation: { maxTokens: 4096 }`) on this request is the sibling of `title.ts:63-68`. #41578 is why `agent.compaction.variant` is also discarded — the agent is never resolved.

`agent.compaction.variant` is ignored because the compaction agent is never resolved onto the request, not because `variant` is dropped later.

The hidden agent exists and even gets a system prompt:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/core/src/plugin/agent.ts#L143-L147

`Agent.ID.make("compaction")` is then used only as a label on the HTTP middleware. The `LLM.request` has no `system` and no agent-derived `variant`:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/core/src/session/compaction.ts#L274-L287

Title generation does the opposite: it loads its hidden agent and passes `agent.info.system` through. Anything under `agent.compaction.*` — `variant`, `system`, model override — is settable config that never reaches the wire.

That is also why #41571 / #42363 get an empty or replayed summary on reasoning models: `no-thinking` cannot be applied, and `PROMPT_COMPACTION` cannot be applied, because nothing reads the agent. One resolve at this call site fixes both.

A local prefix cache (vLLM, llama.cpp, ik_llama.cpp) only survives if the next request starts with the same bytes as the last one: tools, then system, then messages. Two things in this repo change those bytes on purpose.

**Plan ↔ Build changes the tool list.** Tools are built from `registry.snapshot(agent.permissions)`. A blanket-deny permission drops the tool from the request entirely, it is not sent as “disabled”:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/core/src/tool.ts#L205-L214

The tool block is the start of the prefix, so a different list is a full prefill. That matches the Plan→Build stall on ik_llama.cpp and the same symptom in #32603 and #35708.

Claude Code does not do that. It keeps the tool list still and refuses writes at execution time. OpenCode already has that refusal for Plan mode — `edit` / `write` / `patch` die in `execute.before` without touching the wire list:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/core/src/plugin/plan.ts#L33-L38

Advertising the same tools every turn, and keeping that hook, is the fix. Removing tools from the snapshot is what burns the cache.

The Plan reminder is a new synthetic message (`enter` / `leave` on agent switch). If the tool list and system prompt stay put, that is only a short tail. The long stall is the tool-list change. Rewriting an older `<system-reminder>` in place is a separate bust and is #23595.

**Compaction sends a different request under the same session cache key.** Same `promptCacheKey` as the live turn, but `tools: []`, one user message, no system part:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/core/src/session/compaction.ts#L274-L281

That cannot read the cache the session just built, and it writes a divergent prefix onto the key the next Build turn will try to use. On a local engine that is another full prefill.

The repair is to compact as a continuation of the ordinary request — same tools, same system, summarize instruction appended — so the history is a cache read. That is the direction in the comment above, and what #25100 asked for before it was closed for inactivity. #43249 is the same share on hosted prompt-cache.

Keep the tool list still (Claude Code). Compact on top of the live prefix, not beside it. Those two changes are what the local traces are asking for.

The Anthropic merge-normalized-`Usage` risk named here already has a worse sibling on the OpenAI Chat path: usage is **replaced**, not merged.

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/ai/src/protocols/openai-chat.ts#L692

The last chunk that carries any usage object wins outright. A stream that emits `prompt_tokens_details` on one chunk and bare totals on the next drops the cache read/write. Every OpenAI-compatible provider reuses this protocol, so litellm / DeepSeek-compat / GLM-compat all have the same exposure.

Anthropic is the better of the two — it folds per-field:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/ai/src/protocols/anthropic-messages.ts#L709-L716

But it still merges already-normalized `Usage`, which is exactly the gap this issue describes. Accumulating the raw events and normalizing once at `message_stop` / the final Chat chunk fixes both parsers the same way.

`mapUsage` also stashes `providerMetadata: { openai: usage }`. That object is not on the persisted message (105k assistant rows, none carry the key), so a later replay cannot recover the dropped details. The fold has to happen while the stream is still in hand. #34022 is the “cache read is zero” report this replace would produce on a multi-usage stream.

This is fixed for the local CLI and still open for the workerd / Desktop-sidecar path. A heavily used V2 instance (`0.0.0-beta-17498`, 3,246 sessions, 114,870 messages) has:

```
event            0 rows
event_sequence   3,246 rows
page_size 4096 × page_count 462232 → 1.89 GB, almost all in session_message
```

Event persistence became opt-in, default off, in `120e4e7388af61c1b9274b58a16b6e3f9878699c` (“fix(core): make event persistence opt-in”, 2026-08-05). The flag defaults here:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/core/src/bus.ts#L195

One production caller still turns it on — the workerd server:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/9e22c40ffffe82566c00e4a4ad31e7ac3d973d44/packages/server/src/workerd.ts#L69

On that path the 3.2 GB / 90%-events shape in this report is unchanged. `SELECT count(*) FROM event` vs `event_sequence` tells the two installs apart without the version: a fixed CLI is 0 / N, a workerd box is huge / N.

Two things a prune script cannot paper over. There is still no retention on the workerd path (delete is per-aggregate, no TTL). And `PRAGMA auto_vacuum` is NONE, so even a real delete leaves the bytes in the freelist until a `VACUUM` — #31526, measured: deleting half the sessions stranded 855 MB. A community `opencode db prune` that does not `VACUUM` will look like a no-op on disk.

Also confirmed on OpenCode Desktop 1.18.18 on Linux while replacing an old checkout with another clone at a new path.

The new path was inserted into `project_directory`, but `project.worktree` remained the old path. Because both clones had the same Git remote, the new path was also stored in `project.sandboxes` under the same project ID. Selecting the new path therefore normalized back to the old canonical worktree. This overlaps with the shared-remote collision tracked in #42315.

In our case we wanted to completely purge the old OpenCode project and did not need its session history. The tested workaround was:

1. Quit Desktop and back up `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db` plus the relevant files under `~/.config/ai.opencode.desktop/`.
2. Run the deletion with `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON` so deleting the stale shared `project` row also removed its old sessions and directory mappings.
3. Remove the old path from the nested `server`, `globalSync.project`, notification, layout/session, and window-tab state in the Desktop `.dat` files; remove the old path's hashed workspace `.dat` file.
4. Leave the new path as the first/last Desktop project and restart.

Desktop then recreated the project with the new path as `project.worktree`, an empty `sandboxes` list, and no old-path references. The database passed `integrity_check` and `foreign_key_check` afterward.

This is deliberately more destructive than the SQL rebinding workaround already posted above. If session history must be preserved, updating `project.worktree`, `session.directory`, `session.path`, and `project_directory` is preferable. The additional detail from our reproduction is that Desktop's persisted `.dat` state may also need cleanup; changing only the visible project list or only the database can leave the other layer stale.

Confirmed on OpenCode Desktop 1.18.18 on Linux.

We had two clones at different paths with the same basename and the same `origin` URL. After closing clone A and selecting clone B, Desktop reopened clone A. The local database showed exactly the collision described here:

```text
project.worktree = /path/A/repo
project.sandboxes = ["/path/B/repo"]
project_directory = /path/A/repo (main), /path/B/repo
```

Both directories resolved to the same project ID. Closing the project in the Desktop UI only removed sidebar state; it did not remove or replace the canonical `project` row, so selecting B was normalized back to A.

Our tested workaround was intentionally destructive because we no longer needed A or its OpenCode session history:

1. Fully quit Desktop.
2. Back up `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db` with SQLite's `.backup`, plus `~/.config/ai.opencode.desktop/opencode.global.dat`, the active `opencode.window.*.dat`, and A's hashed `opencode.workspace.*.dat`.
3. Enable foreign keys and delete the shared project row from `opencode.db`. This cascades to its sessions, messages, permissions, and both `project_directory` mappings.
4. Remove A from the nested `server` and `globalSync.project` state in `opencode.global.dat`, remove A's notification/layout/session cache entries, remove its window tab entry, and remove A's hashed workspace state file.
5. Keep B as `server.projects.local[0]` and `lastProject.local`, then restart Desktop.

On restart, OpenCode recreated the same Git-derived project ID with:

```text
project.worktree = /path/B/repo
project.sandboxes = []
```

There were no remaining A directory/session/cache references, and Desktop opened B normally.

Important: deleting the shared project row removes session history for that project ID, so this workaround is only appropriate when the old history can be discarded. Editing `opencode.global.dat` alone was not enough because the stale canonical path also lived in `opencode.db`.

Tried to reproduce this against current `v2` tip (`4b9d89e94`, "refactor(core): move image config into state") with `effect@4.0.0-beta.107` (the version pinned at #43109, unchanged since #43172 landed) and could not see a required `sessionID` on either side of the contract:

- **Generated contract** — replicating `packages/core/src/tool/runtime.ts` `toJsonSchema()` (including `flattenAllOf` / `inlineLocalReferences` / `dropDefinitionsIfResolved`) over the exact `Input` from `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/subagent.ts` (branded `SessionSchema.ID` + `.annotate`, as registered via `ctx.tool.transform().add()`), the JSON Schema sent to providers comes out as `required: ["agent", "description", "prompt"]` — `sessionID` and `background` are correctly optional.
- **Decode path** — `Schema.decodeUnknownEffect(Input)({ agent: "explore" })` (what `runtime.ts` `decodeInput` runs on an omitted value) accepts the call without a `sessionID`.

Could you share which surface showed `sessionID` as required (provider tool listing, web UI inspector, SDK types, or a rejected tool call), and the exact commit your `beta-17595` build was cut from? If the blocked call came from a provider rejecting an omitted argument, the request payload for that one call would pin down whether the required-ness is being injected somewhere between `runtime.ts` `definition()` and the provider adapter.

Found the line, so this should be quick to fix — `packages/schema/src/identifier.ts`:

```js
const current = BigInt(timestamp) * 0x1000n + BigInt(counter)
const value = descending ? ~current : current
const time = Array.from({ length: 6 }, (_, index) =>
  Number((value >> BigInt(40 - 8 * index)) & 0xffn).toString(16).padStart(2, "0"),
).join("")
```

`timestamp * 0x1000` is about 7.3e15 for a 2026 date, which needs 53 bits, but only 6 bytes are rendered. The top 5 bits are dropped, so what actually survives is a 36-bit millisecond field — which is where the ~795 day period comes from, and it matches the `(time_ms mod 2^36) * 4096 + counter` fit in the issue exactly. The `~current` on the descending branch is why session ids sort the other way and wrapped at the same instant.

Widening the render to 8 bytes would push the next rollover past any horizon that matters, at the cost of longer ids. Keeping 6 bytes and subtracting a fixed epoch would preserve the length and buy another ~795 years, but changes how existing ids compare against new ones, so it needs a migration story. Making `create` refuse to go backwards against the last issued id would at least make it fail loudly rather than silently reorder history.

For what it is worth, the file has not changed since #33571 on 24 June, and that was a refactor that only moved it, so this has been latent since well before the rollover rather than a recent regression.

Additional macOS data point on 1.18.18, measured read-only while opencode was running: 7.0 GB database, event 5,392 MB of it (83%), 384,496 rows.

Largest event: 77,177,325 bytes, one of four near-identical snapshots of the same message. `$.info.summary.diffs` is 77,177,003 of those bytes — 99.9996% — across 9,029 entries, individual patches up to 1.9 MB.

The trigger looks new to this thread. All 9,029 entries are under `app/node_modules/`. `node_modules/` is gitignored in that repository, but the rule was added in that same session's own commit — the session installed the frontend toolchain, and `summary.diffs` was computed in the window before the rule existed. So the worst case isn't only a function of legitimate diff volume; it's reachable by transiently-unignored generated trees.

That suggests a bound worth having alongside the side-table eviction in #42771: have `summary.diffs` honour ignore rules, and cap per-file patch bytes and entry count. Eviction addresses the write rate; a cap addresses the worst single payload, which is what produced the 77 MB row here.
